Stage 3 · Grammar

Putting the events in order

Five small words that tell the listener exactly when things happened.

Read these four sentences about the balloon story.
  • As soon as it was high in the sky, they called the police.
  • Helicopters tracked it until they found a safe way down.
  • By the time it landed, the story was live on television.
  • While reporters were interviewing the family, the boy said too much.
Which one means “immediately after”?
Linkers tell your listener whether things happened one after another, or at the same time.

Two clauses joined by and tell you almost nothing about timing. The same two clauses joined by as soon as, while or by the time produce three quite different stories. Time linkers are how English encodes the relationship between events, and choosing the right one is part of telling a story accurately rather than merely correctly.

The set divides naturally by meaning. Some linkers express sequence: as soon as (immediately after), when (at that point), before and after (explicit order). Some express overlap: while and as, which introduce a longer action, usually in the past continuous. And some express a boundary: until marks where a continuing situation stopped, and by the time marks a deadline by which something was already complete.

Alongside these conjunctions sits a second group that behaves differently: the adverbials then, meanwhile, in the end, eventually, finally. These are not conjunctions and cannot join two clauses on their own. Meanwhile starts a new sentence and takes a comma; writing Meanwhile she waited, he drove home is a punctuation error, not a stylistic choice.

One rule cuts across the whole set and is worth fixing in your mind now, because it also governs the conditionals later in the course: after a time conjunction, English does not use a future form, even when the meaning is clearly future. I’ll call you as soon as I arrive — never as soon as I will arrive. The future is already carried by the main clause.

Before you look at the table: the table below groups the linkers by the relationship they express — sequence, overlap or boundary — and shows the comma rule. Learn them by relationship, not alphabetically.
One linker per column
LinkerWhat it says about the orderUsual form after itExample
whenat that moment, or just afterpast simpleWhen the boy was not found, a search started.
whileduring a longer action that was already going onpast continuousWhile he was looking for the path, he fell.
as soon asimmediately afterpast simpleAs soon as it was high in the sky, they phoned.
by the timebefore that point, everything had already happenedoften past perfect in the other clauseBy the time the hoax was discovered, they had wasted forty years.
untilup to that point, then it stoppedpast simpleThey tracked it until they found a safe way down.

Two clauses, one comma rule. If the linker comes first, put a comma in the middle: As soon as it landed, everyone ran over. If it comes second, no comma: Everyone ran over as soon as it landed.

By the time pulls the past perfect with it. It means “before that moment”, so the other clause usually steps back: By the time we arrived, the shop had closed.

The mistake to avoid. Until cannot start a sentence on its own: not Until I saw it. It needs both halves: I didn’t believe it until I saw it.

One more. While goes with the long action and when with the short one. While I was cooking, the phone rang — not the other way round.

Full grammar reference — time linkers — sequencing the events of a story

What it is

Time linkers are conjunctions and adverbials that show how two events relate in time: which came first, whether they overlapped, and where one ended. The main set at this level is when, while, as, as soon as, by the time, until, before, after, plus the adverbial markers then, meanwhile, in the end, eventually, finally.

What it means, and what it does

Linkers do the work that the tense alone cannot. Two past simple clauses joined by and tell you almost nothing about timing; the same two clauses joined by as soon as, while or by the time produce three quite different stories. Choosing the linker is choosing the relationship — sequence, overlap, or deadline.

When and why we use it

Two clauses joined by and tell you almost nothing about timing. The same two clauses joined by as soon as, while or by the time produce three quite different stories. Time linkers are how English encodes the relationship between events, and choosing the right one is part of telling a story accurately rather than merely correctly.

The set divides naturally by meaning. Some linkers express sequence: as soon as (immediately after), when (at that point), before and after (explicit order). Some express overlap: while and as, which introduce a longer action, usually in the past continuous. And some express a boundary: until marks where a continuing situation stopped, and by the time marks a deadline by which something was already complete.

Alongside these conjunctions sits a second group that behaves differently: the adverbials then, meanwhile, in the end, eventually, finally. These are not conjunctions and cannot join two clauses on their own. Meanwhile starts a new sentence and takes a comma; writing Meanwhile she waited, he drove home is a punctuation error, not a stylistic choice.

One rule cuts across the whole set and is worth fixing in your mind now, because it also governs the conditionals later in the course: after a time conjunction, English does not use a future form, even when the meaning is clearly future. I’ll call you as soon as I arrive — never as soon as I will arrive. The future is already carried by the main clause.

Typical situations

You need time linkers for narrating events, giving instructions in order, explaining a process, reporting news and describing a sequence of changes. They also appear constantly in the reading and listening texts of this level.

  • One event immediately after another — as soon as stresses that no time passed in between.As soon as I pressed Send, I knew it was a mistake.
  • One event during another — while and as introduce the longer action, normally in the continuous.While he was looking for the path, he fell.
  • A point in time — when is the neutral option — it works for both a point and a period.When the police were informed, helicopters were sent up.
  • An earlier deadline — by the time means ‘not later than the moment when’, and usually pulls the past perfect into the other clause.By the time the hoax was discovered, scientists had wasted forty years.
  • The end point of a situation — until marks the moment a continuing situation stopped.We lived in Warsaw until I was twelve.
  • Explicit order — before and after state the order directly, so the past perfect is often unnecessary.He checked the rope before he climbed.
  • Moving the narrative on — adverbial markers, which are not conjunctions and take a comma.Meanwhile, she was waiting at the bus station. In the end, nobody came.

How it differs from similar structures

while or when? While needs a period of time and normally a continuous verb. When works for a period or a single point, which is why it is safer if you are unsure.
until or by the time? Until = right up to that moment, then it stops. By the time = at some point before that moment, it was already done.

How to build it

Conjunction, front position: As soon as + clause, + main clause
Conjunction, mid position: main clause + as soon as + clause  (no comma)
Adverbial: Meanwhile, / In the end, / Then + main clause
Two clauses, either orderWhile she was reading, the phone rang. = The phone rang while she was reading.
Comma ruleComma only when the linker clause comes first: By the time we arrived, it had closed.
NegativeHe didn’t say anything until she asked.
QuestionWhat were you doing when it happened?
With the past perfectBy the time the story reached the news, the boy had already admitted it.
Adverbials are not conjunctionsShe waited. Meanwhile, he was driving home. — two sentences, not one.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • When + past simple and when + past continuous mean different things. When the alarm rang, I left (I left afterwards) vs When the alarm rang, I was leaving (I was already on my way).
  • After as soon as, when, until, by the time, before, after, English does not use a future form even about the future: I’ll call you as soon as I arrive, never as soon as I will arrive.
  • Until answers how long?; by answers when at the latest? I’ll be here until six (the whole time) vs I’ll be here by six (I will have arrived).
  • Meanwhile and in the meantime are adverbs, not conjunctions. They cannot join two clauses on their own.
  • At last expresses relief; finally and in the end are neutral; at the end refers to a place in something (at the end of the film), not to time.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • As soon as I will finish, I’ll call you. → As soon as I finish, I’ll call you.No future form after a time conjunction.
  • While I read the report, he called. → While I was reading the report, he called.While introduces the longer background action.
  • By the time we arrived, the film started. → By the time we arrived, the film had started.By the time looks back at something already complete.
  • I waited until he will come. → I waited until he came.Until takes a past form in a past story.
  • Meanwhile she was waiting, he drove home. → Meanwhile, she was waiting. He drove home.Meanwhile is an adverb and cannot join two clauses.
  • In the end of the story he escaped. → In the end, he escaped.At the end of refers to a place; in the end means finally.

More examples in context

  • immediateAs soon as the police arrived, the crowd disappeared.
  • overlapWhile the reporters were interviewing the family, the boy mentioned the truth.
  • point in timeWhen the balloon landed, the story was already live on television.
  • deadlineBy the time the hoax was discovered, nearly forty years had passed.
  • end pointNobody suspected anything until a scientist looked at the teeth.
  • explicit orderHe invented the whole thing before he told the newspaper.
  • afterAfter the interview finished, the family changed their story.
  • parallel actionThe helicopters searched the sky. Meanwhile, the boy was hiding at home.
  • outcomeIn the end, it turned out that the parents had made it up.
  • future time clauseI’ll tell you the rest when I see you.

A tip for remembering it

Test a linker by asking one question. Did one thing stop the other? → when / as soon as. Were they both going on together? → while / as. Was it already finished by then? → by the time + past perfect. How long did it continue? → until.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Time linkers show sequence, overlap or a deadline — the tense alone cannot.
  2. As soon as = immediately after; while / as = during; by the time = already complete before.
  3. A linker clause at the front takes a comma; at the end it takes none.
  4. Never use will after when, as soon as, until, before, after, by the time.
  5. Until answers how long; by answers at the latest when.
  6. Meanwhile, in the end, finally are adverbs: they start a new sentence, they do not join clauses.

Stage 5 · Main input

Too good to be true

Three famous hoaxes, and how each of them came apart.

Before you read: you will read about three stories that turned out to be false.

Which do you think spread fastest?

Decide first. The text answers this directly in the last two paragraphs.

Too good to be true

Three stories that millions of people believed. One took forty years to unravel; another lasted a single afternoon.

AIn December 1912 a lawyer named Charles Dawson announced that he had found something remarkable in a gravel pit in the south of England: a skull with a human forehead and an ape-like jaw. Scientists were keen to find evidence that would prove the link between early man and apes, and here it was. The find was reported around the world. Museums put it on display. It was named Piltdown Man.

BBy the time the hoax was discovered, scientists had wasted nearly forty years believing a lie. In 1953 a team of researchers tested the bones properly and reached an uncomfortable conclusion: the skull was human and modern, the jaw belonged to an orangutan, and the teeth had been filed down and stained to match. Meanwhile Dawson, who most people now consider responsible for making the fake, had died. Nobody was ever charged.

CNot every hoax takes forty years. On 15 October 2009 the media reported that a six-year-old boy was inside a large silver balloon floating high in the sky above Colorado. The police were informed and helicopters were sent up to track it. By the time the balloon finally landed about eighty kilometres away, an hour or so later, the story was live on television and millions of people were watching.

DThe boy was not in the balloon. He was at home, hiding in the family garage. That evening, while reporters were interviewing the family on live television, he accidentally mentioned that they had done it “for the show”. The whole story had been made up by his parents in an attempt to get a reality TV deal. As soon as the interview ended, the police reopened the case.

EHoaxes travel faster than they used to. Before the internet, a false story needed a newspaper. Now a picture circulates in minutes: a bright blue watermelon that supposedly changes the taste of everything you eat afterwards, or a claim that dialling the emergency number will charge your phone battery. That second one caused real harm. Police announced that calls to 999 had risen sharply, and told the public to ignore the hoax and keep the line free.

FSo why do we believe? Researchers who study this point to two things. First, a good hoax gives people what they already expect — Piltdown Man arrived exactly when scientists were looking for it. Second, checking takes effort, and sharing takes none. Until that changes, the next story that seems too good to be true will still reach a few million screens before anyone thinks to ask.

Written for this course. The Piltdown Man, Loch Ness and balloon-boy cases are documented in the archives of the Natural History Museum, London, and in contemporary news reporting.
